c.tagline: Endless beaches, craft beer, and year-round sunshine.

taxi.fareNote: Metered taxis are available but ride-hailing apps are far more common; from the airport most travelers use Uber, Lyft, or a shuttle rather than a cab.

emergency.note: 911 is the single emergency number for police, fire, and ambulance across the United States.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Very safe; caution in some areas at night; car break-ins near beaches

hood_desc: The walkable Victorian-era heart of downtown, packed with restaurants, rooftop bars, clubs, and the convention center; the go-to base for first-timers who want nightlife and dining on their doorstep.

An upscale seaside enclave of coves, cliffs, and sea-lion beaches with the Birch Aquarium, boutiques, and the Museum of Contemporary Art; suits travelers wanting scenery, snorkeling, and refined dining.
A compact, trendy waterfront district of Italian trattorias, craft cocktail bars, design shops, and the weekly Mercato farmers market; popular with foodies and younger travelers.
San Diego's craft-beer and hipster capital, full of indie breweries, vintage shops, coffee roasters, and murals; draws a creative, bohemian, twenty- and thirty-something crowd.
A quiet, resort-like island (technically a peninsula) across the bay, home to the landmark Hotel del Coronado, wide family beaches, and manicured streets; ideal for a relaxed, upscale stay.
lodging: Courtyard by Marriott San Diego Downtown Little Italy
The Lafayette Hotel, Swim Club & Bungalows

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink, though some prefer filtered for taste.

transit.hours: Trolley lines run roughly 4:30am to around 1am; the UC San Diego Blue Line runs 24 hours on weekends. Buses vary by route, with limited late-night service.
transit.note: MTS runs the San Diego Trolley (light rail) plus an extensive bus network; the separate Coaster commuter train links downtown north to Oceanside along the coast.
transit.pay: Tap a reloadable PRONTO card or the PRONTO app at fare readers on trolleys and buses. A single ride is $2.50, and fares cap at $6 per day / $12 per week of actual rides, so you never pay more than a day or week pass.

tip.r: 15-20% at restaurants is the norm; tipping is expected for most service in the US.

food.name: Baja fish taco
food.desc: Beer-battered or grilled white fish in a corn tortilla with cabbage, crema and lime. Brought north from Ensenada and perfected here.

places.name: Oscar's Mexican Seafood
places.note: Routinely called the city's best; the smoked fish taco is the sleeper order.

places.name: TJ Oyster Bar
places.note: Small, cheap and beloved by local chefs; crunchy battered tilapia and outstanding smoked tuna.

places.name: The Taco Stand
places.note: Tortillas pressed on site and a good salsa bar; the most reliable option for first-timers.

food.name: California burrito
food.desc: Carne asada, french fries, cheese and guacamole in a flour tortilla. Invented in San Diego and essentially unavailable done right anywhere else.

places.name: Lolita's Mexican Food
places.note: The consensus champion; skinny-cut fries keep their crunch, and their carne asada fries top every local poll.

places.name: Nico's Mexican Food
places.note: Classic late-night taco shop near the beach; unpretentious and consistently good.

places.name: Roberto's Taco Shop
places.note: The original San Diego taco-shop family, many branches open 24 hours; the default 2am burrito.

food.name: Carne asada tacos
food.desc: Mesquite-grilled, chopped skirt or ribeye on house-made tortillas with guacamole and grilled onion. The border-city benchmark dish.

places.name: Tacos El Gordo
places.note: Tijuana original, order at separate stations by meat; adobada and cabeza are as good as the asada.

places.name: Salud!
places.note: Michelin-recognised neighbourhood taqueria with house-made tortillas and strong local art-scene atmosphere.

places.name: Las Cuatro Milpas
places.note: Family-run since 1933, cash only, lunch hours only, and a queue down the block. Worth it.

food.name: Birria
food.desc: Chile-braised beef or goat, served as quesatacos with consomme for dipping. San Diego's proximity to Tijuana makes it a serious birria town.

places.name: Aqui es Texcoco
places.note: Specialises in wood-pit lamb barbacoa and consomme rather than the trendy beef version; a genuine destination.

places.name: Wet Tacos
places.note: Grass-fed halal beef birria from a truck; named the city's best in a month-long local search.

food.name: Ceviche and mariscos tostadas
food.desc: Shrimp aguachile, smoked marlin and lime-cured fish piled on tostadas, eaten standing at trucks and counters near the bay.

places.name: Mariscos El Pescador
places.note: Cult seafood truck for ceviche de camaron tostadas and green aguachile; cash is easiest.

places.name: Karina's Ceviches and More
places.note: Long-running local mini-chain with a big raw-bar list and reliable quality.

places.name: Todo Pa' La Cruda
places.note: Hangover-cure specialists; loud, casual and packed with locals at weekends.

food.name: West Coast IPA
food.desc: Bone-dry, resinous, pine-and-citrus IPA. San Diego effectively invented the modern style and has well over 150 breweries.

places.name: Societe Brewing Company
places.note: The Pupil has been the local aficionados' benchmark IPA for more than a decade; also strong Belgian-style beers.

places.name: AleSmith Brewing Company
places.note: Big, welcoming tasting room with a Tony Gwynn museum; Speedway Stout is the other must-try.

places.name: Pizza Port
places.note: The 1980s brewpub that helped start it all; Swami's IPA with a slice, feet still sandy.

food.name: Margarita
food.desc: Tequila, lime and orange liqueur, taken seriously in a city with deep agave knowledge and no shortage of tequilerias.

places.name: Tahona Bar
places.note: Housemade triple sec and fresh lime in a straightforward house marg that outclasses the tourist competition.

places.name: El Agave Restaurant and Tequileria
places.note: Enormous agave collection lining the walls; go for a sipping flight as well as the margarita.

places.name: Lola 55
places.note: Michelin Bib Gourmand taco bar built around cocktails; mezcal and tequila drinks match the food.

landmarks: Balboa Park
A sprawling cultural park anchored by Spanish Colonial Revival architecture, home to the San Diego Zoo and numerous museums, offering some of the city's most photographed facades.
USS Midway Museum
A decommissioned WWII-era aircraft carrier turned floating museum on the waterfront, famous for its flight deck views and the iconic 'Unconditional Surrender' sculpture nearby.
Coronado Bridge
A dramatic curving suspension bridge arching over San Diego Bay, prized by photographers for its sweeping lines against the skyline.
Hotel del Coronado
A historic Victorian beachfront resort famed for its red-turreted architecture and status as one of America's most photographed grand hotels.
Cabrillo National Monument
A dramatic cliffside site at the tip of Point Loma offering panoramic views of the bay, ocean, and skyline alongside a historic lighthouse.
La Jolla Cove
A picturesque cove with turquoise waters, sea caves, and resident sea lions, ranked among the most beautiful urban coastlines in the world.
Torrey Pines State Natural Reserve
Rugged sandstone cliffs and rare pine forests overlooking the Pacific, a favorite for dramatic sunset photography.
San Diego Zoo
One of the world's most renowned zoos, set in lush Balboa Park and famous for its pioneering open-air enclosures and giant panda legacy.
Old Town San Diego
The birthplace of California, this historic district preserves adobe buildings and Mexican-era charm evoking the city's earliest days.
Sunset Cliffs Natural Park
Wave-carved sandstone bluffs along the Pacific renowned for producing some of San Diego's most spectacular sunset photographs.

train.note: No passenger train crosses into Mexico - the old San Diego and Arizona line into Tijuana carries freight only. Amtrak's Pacific Surfliner is the intercity service, leaving Santa Fe Depot at 1050 Kettner Boulevard downtown for Los Angeles in about 2 hours 45 minutes and continuing to Santa Barbara and San Luis Obispo. NCTD's Coaster commuter trains run up the coast to Oceanside, where you can change to Metrolink for Orange County and Los Angeles, often much cheaper than through Amtrak fares. The MTS Blue Line trolley runs from downtown to the San Ysidro border crossing in around 40 minutes, which is how most people reach Tijuana.

bus.note: Domestic coaches leave from the stop beside Santa Fe Depot: Greyhound (https://www.greyhound.com/), FlixBus (https://www.flixbus.com/) and Megabus (https://us.megabus.com/) all serve Los Angeles in 2.5-3 hours and continue to Las Vegas and Phoenix. For Mexico, most travellers ride the Blue Line trolley to San Ysidro and walk across the border, then pick up Mexican long-distance coaches at Tijuana's Central de Autobuses. Mexicoach runs hourly buses from San Ysidro to Avenida Revolucion and the Tijuana bus station for about $7, saving the walk. Carry a passport in both directions - northbound queues back into the US can run to two hours at peak times.

intl.to: Coronado (USA) - from the Broadway Pier and Fifth Avenue Landing downtown

ferry.note: There are no international ferries; the old passenger sailings to Ensenada and Catalina no longer operate. The Coronado Ferry crosses San Diego Bay from the Broadway Pier and Fifth Avenue Landing to the Coronado Ferry Landing in about 15 minutes, running roughly hourly through the day - it is a foot-passenger and bicycle service with no vehicle deck, so no advance booking is needed. Flagship's terminal at 990 North Harbor Drive is a short walk from Santa Fe Depot. Cruise ships use the B Street Cruise Terminal nearby, but those are round-trip voyages rather than point-to-point transport.

half.name: Tijuana
half.blurb: A border city reached on foot or by trolley, known for Avenida Revolución, street tacos, and the Centro Cultural Tijuana.

half.name: Julian
half.blurb: A former gold-mining town in the Cuyamaca Mountains known for apple orchards, pie shops, and a small historic main street.

half.name: Temecula
half.blurb: A wine region of rolling vineyards and tasting rooms in inland Riverside County, about an hour northeast of the city.

half.name: Anza-Borrego Desert State Park
half.blurb: California's largest state park, with slot canyons, badlands, and spring wildflower blooms across the Colorado Desert.
